THE LATE MR. J. K. FLEMMING Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):	Before the orders of the
day are called may I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to make mention of a loss this House has sustained, and which at the moment is much in the minds of all present. For the third time, in the brief interval which has elapsed since this parliament assembled, we have been called upon to pause in the proceedings of this House and refer to the death of one of our number. The speech from the throne had just been read when we learned of the death of an hon. member from the province of Nova Scotia. At the beginning of the present week we had occasion to refer, as we reassembled after our brief recess, to the death of another honourable member, this time from Ontario. And to-day, ere the week is over, we are called upon to record the death of yet another of our number, an hon. member from the province of New Brunswick. All three were present with us and took their seats at the opening of the present session, the proceedings of which have

only thus far little more than commenced. I do not believe that in the history of our parliament the House of Commons has been called upon to mourn in so brief a space of time the loss of so many of its members; certainly never before were like losses in its membership sustained upon the very threshold of a new parliament.
The Hon. J. K. Flemming, whose death occurred yesterday, was the member for Carleton-Victoria. He entered this parliament at the general elections of 1925 and was present through the greater part of last session, which, as is well known, was also the last parliament. He was returned again at the general elections of 1926. Though in parliament but a short time he was a conspicuous figure, having some years ago occupied the position of premier of his native province. Though faithful in his attendance in this House, his voice was not heard on more than one or two occasions, partly no doubt because it was his first session in the federal parliament and partly due no doubt also to the ill-health from which he suffered. In the short time he was here, his kindly and pleasing personality won for him many friends among men of all parties.
The Hon. Mr. Flemming was born in Carleton county on April 27, 1868. His life was, for the most part, identified with the county of his birth and the affairs of his native province, of which, in the year 1911, he became the premier. After receiving an education at the common schools, he graduated from the provincial Normal school and followed for a time the profession of teaching. Later he engaged in commercial and industrial pursuits. For a time he was a travelling salesman and merchant; subsequently he became actively interested in lumbering operations and the development of the lumbering industry.
Mr. Flemming was a leader of the Conservative party -in the province of New Brunswick. Practically all his life he took an active interest in public affairs. He encountered at the outset two defeats in his candidature for the legislature of his province. That was in 1895 and 1899, but in a by-election in 1900 he was returned to the legislature; and from that time on his rise to prominence in the affairs of his province w.as unbroken and rapid. He was re-elected to the legislature in 1903 and 1908. In the latter year he became Provincial Secretary and Receiver General in the cabinet of Sir Douglas-then Mr.-Hazen, and on the resignation of Sir Douglas Hazen in 1911, when Mr. Hazen entered the cabinet of Sir Robert Borden, Mr. Flemming succeeded to the premiership

of the province; this position he held until the close of 1913, at *which time, suffering from ill-health, he resigned both the premiership and his seat in the legislature.
From 1914 until 1925, when he was nominated to contest Victoria-Carleton in the interests of the Conservative party and was returned as member to this parliament, Mr. Flemming had practically retired from active politics. Whilst to some extent he regained his health and strength, he nevertheless suffered one or two serious illnesses during this period of retirement and hon. members who were with him in this parliament at the last session will recall that he suffered considerably at times through the impairment of his health. When, therefore, it was learned a few days ago that he had again to undergo an operation there were many who greatly feared the outcome.
May I, speaking for hon. members on this side of the House, say that we join with hon. gentlemen opposite in greatly regretting the less which the House has sustained, and which will be particularly felt by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition and those who support him; and that we share with them the sympathy which we hope you, Mr. Speaker, will kindly convey, in the name of the Commons as a whole, to the widow and sons and daughters of our late colleague, who have been so greatly bereaved.

speakeroldname: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of those
who sit on your left in this chamber, may I thank my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for the befitting and generous tribute which he has just paid to the memory of one whom we held in great respect, whom we held very dearly in this quarter of the chamber. I did not know the late Mr. Flemming personally until he came here for the first time about two years ago; but one was at once struck with his ability, with his kindheartedness, with his wonderful fund of information in regard to public affairs in this country. What struck me most was that even as far back as a year or two ago he seemed to have himself a realization that he was afflicted with some malady which would in the near or distant future result fatally. He told me last session that his health was rapidly failing and he did not know how long he would be able to continue. But he always exhibited patience, cheerfulness and courage, although he was well aware that the vital forces were daily growing weaker and weaker.
He was a man of outstanding ability, a very able speaker, an excellent debater, a man who had risen to the highest position in his native province, and who, had he been spared in this
chamber, would have proved to be one of the ablest and most useful of our membership. But during all the time that he sat in this chamber I am satisfied that he had a hard fight against the ill health which constantly pursued him. I am sure that the whole chamber will deeply regret his death. We on this side realize that we have suffered a tremendous loss. We have lost a political friend, a personal friend, and a great ally in the Conservative party.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the members who sit in this comer of the chamber, may I say that we desire to be associated with the message of sympathy and condolence to be expressed to the widow and other relatives of the late Mr. Flemming. We particularly in this corner did not know Mr. Flemming very well, but he always seemed to us to be very cheerful and we thought he was in fairly good health. Circumstances have decreed otherwise, and we in this comer of the chamber, as we all must, very much regret his loss. We desire, therefore, to be associated with this message of sympathy.

speechtext: Is the Minist.iv of Immigration aware that agents for the Canadian National Railways are offering guaranteed employment to immigrants to this country and that some of those who have been guaranteed employment are now in absolute destitution in the cities of western Canada? speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT FORKE (Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speechtext: I have no information of any destitution anywhere in the Dominion at the present time.

May I not secure

I think it is only fair that I should have an answer as to what can be done by the Immigration department when a serious state of affairs such as this exists, when men are coming to this country under an agreement that they are to be provided with work-I have a printed copy here to that effect-and then when they get here become a burden upon our cities.

If the hon. gentleman had
given me a little notice that he was going to ask this question I would have been able to reply to him much more fully. I am a new minister just starting out, and I was taken a little by surprise. I have heard that there has been unemployment in some of the towns in Canada. speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) interrogated the Prime Minister yesterday in respect to the agitation going on in British Columbia in connection with Indian title and I did not happen to be in the House on the occasion of the interrogation. speechtext:
Yes. During all that period we have endeavoured by negotiation and conference to see if a settlement could not be reached. But we have been making a special study of the whole question, because the provincial government, the federal government and the Indians are all interested in the matter. The representatives of the Indian tribes are pressing for a judicial investigation of the whole question of Indian title and asking that the matter be carried to the Privy Council.

That request has not been granted, although it is receiving consideration. We have a committee of the government acting in cooperation with the Deputy Minister of Justice, working on the situation and endeavouring to reach a decision as to whether or not it would be wise to submit the matter for judicial investigation, with the privilege of carrying the whole question to the Privy Council.

Might I ask the minister if he has given consideration to my suggestion that a small select committee of parliament be appointed to consider the matter? speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have given that matter some consideration, but we have already spent a great deal of money in bringing witnesses from British Columbia, and I really do not believe that any new evidence can be submitted; there are volumes of evidence already. If a committee of parliament would be helpful, without going to the expense of bringing two or three hundred witnesses from British Columblia, I would be inclined to ask for that assistance, but there has been so much investigation already, so much evidence taken and so much money spent on this controversial question, that I am inclined to think we had better have a try at a solution of the problem by the present committee and see if we cannot get together. We have managed to settle some of the more difficult problems that were engaging our attention. I do not say that we shall settle this one, but we at least want to make a little further attempt to settle it.
I earnestly hope the minister will be able to settle it.

speechtext:
For the benefit of
those of us who have had no legal training I hope the minister will explain bow this arrangement can be forced upon individual bondholders. It looks to me like the confiscation of their existing bonds and the substitution of something else whether the individual bondholder may be agreeable or not. I understood the minister to say yesterday that this was not a matter of charity or of a compassionate allowance; he stated that these individuals had a legal claim. Well, if they have a legal claim, how can that claim be superseded in the way here proposed? If one individual bondholder undertakes to stand out, how can he be forced to come into the scheme? And if he can be forced into the scheme, then it is worth considering whether or not we are right in proceeding with the arrangement. If there is nothing legally binding on us in this regard it seems to me that the other question which was discussed yesterday must come up again. These people gave bonds for a concern that proved bankrupt and the Dominion came to the resuce and stood behind the railway. Now it appears that we are to honour all the claims that exist in regard to this unsuccessful railway. Why should we do so if we are under no legal obligation? These are questions that should be clearly explained before we adopt this legislation. We were told yesterday of one instance in which one party signed the contract while the other declined to do so. It seems to me that in this case the Dominion is signing. How shall we force the other people to sign if they do not want to do so?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
My bon. friend's premise regarding the situation of the company in relation to the government is scarcely cor-

rect. I said yesterday, and I repeat it to-day, that these people hold in their hand an absolute security having behind it terms enforceable in the courts of the country against first, the Grand Trunk Pacific which, as my hon. friend says, is a bankrupt concern in receivership. I have the unpleasant privilege of being the receiver for the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Grand Trunk Railway, however, cannot be placed in the same class at all, and in the bonds held by these people there is a provision of guarantee by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. Now the Grand Trunk Railway has other legal obligations ranking prior to this one, and if in any year the Grand Trunk Railway earns more than sufficient to pay those prior obligations and has any money over, then these people have a legal claim against the former Grand Trunk Railway for their four per cent interest.
As to the other point dealing with minorities who do not assent, I remarked a little while ago that we had had the assent of ninety-two per cent of the bondholders. I am told that it is unique that there should be such a large proportion of assent in connection with an arrangement of this kind.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Is that a binding assent?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
Absolutely binding; it is
a signed assent. Now there must always be some machinery for clearing up matters of this kind, otherwise business could not be conducted. That is recognized in our Exchequer Court Act and in the Railway Act, whereby provisions are made generally to deal with the liquidation of bonds of railway companies. The Railway Act provides that the Exchequer Court may give permission to bind what my hon. friend refers to as a minority in case seventy-five per cent of the whole consent. And in view of the fact that in this case we had already in hand a ninety-two per cent approval we thought it unnecessary to involve the legal machinery of the Exchequer court which, as I have said, is authorized under our existing laws to bind the others in the event of seventy-five per cent consenting. That is the best answer I can give my hon. friend. If there were not some means of cleaning up the tag ends no bond issue could ever be dealt with because there is always a proportion of bonds which simply cannot be located. Bonds vanish, they go out of existence, they are burnt up in fires or they go down with ships. As a matter of fact I am of opinion that with such a large percentage agreeing we may say that practically all the existing bondholders have given their consent.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
I am not perfectly
clear in regard to the interpretation of the percentages. Section 3 provides:
The scheme of arrangement having already been assented to in writing by the holders of three-fourths in value of the Pacific stock-
That is altogether different from saying, "three-fourths of the holders of the stock". The minister says that ninety-two per cent of approximately seven thousand bondholders have given assent. Does he mean the holders of ninety-two per cent of the stock or ninety-two per cent of the holders of the stock?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
Ninety-two per cent "in
value".

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
That is a different
thing from ninety-two per cent of the individual bondholders. I can well conceive that ten or twelve bondholders may hold seventy-five per cent of the stock and that a large majority of the bondholders may be coerced into doing what the minority wish them to do, simply because that minority hold a majority of the stock. Is that the situation?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: My hon. friend is suggesting a purely hypothetical possibility; it is remotely possible. I am sure however that had there been any such coercion we should have heard about it, for the reason that this matter has been discussed in the press, particularly in investors' journals in the old land, for years past; and the scheme of arrangement itself was widely advertised months ago, each bondholder having been personally apprised of the fact that the scheme contains a provision that it shall bcome operative when assented to by three-fourths of the bondholders. That is what the bondholders were asked to consent to as part of the scheme of arrangement.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Has the minister the information as to what percentage of actual bondholders have subscribed to the agreement?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: I am afraid I have not that information.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Was this original bond issue secured by a trust deed?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Or a statutory mortgage?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Statutory stock, yes.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: And does this arrangement depart from the conditions of the statute in any other respect?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Well then, I do not think the point raised by our laymen friends was very well taken. If ninety-two per cent in value of the bondholders have agreed, that is a very large proportion of any body of bondholders. Usually the proportion is very much less.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Very much.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Sometimes it is only sixty per cent.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Yes, and less than that.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: I should like the minister to correct me if I am wrong in the supposition that by this legislation we are deliberately depriving the holders of this debenture stock, who may not have signed the agreement, of any rights which they may have, except what we now give them in this way?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: That is correct.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Would it not be much better to follow the usual procedure and ask the Exchequer court to make this ruling? Because I understand that one reason why we are putting this agreement through is to help the condition of Canadian credit in London. There is a feeling there that we have not treated these bondholders properly. Is it not possible that some of these bondholders would not approve of this scheme, and will have the right to say that the parliament of Canada has deliberately by legislation taken their debenture stock which calls for four per cent interest and give them two per cent? It does seem as though they might consider we are doing something very drastic to interfere with the security which they hold, and in that case they certainly could say much against Canada because this parliament is deliberately putting through this legislation.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
The point my hon. friend raises was a point of difficulty with myself in considering the scheme, that is as between myself and officers of the company. The element of time is of very great importance in connection with this matter, because of the very near arrival of another interest date on these bonds, and the arrangement which is accepted, as I say, by ninety-two per cent of the bondholders, provides in clause 9 (b) that the scheme shall become operative when the same has been confirmed by the Exchequer court of Canada if such confirmation
216	COMMONS
Grand Trunk Pacific Ry. Co.
shall be required by the company. That is to say the bondholders themselves agreed to waive confirmation by the Exchequer court, provided the company did not require it for some purpose of its own. Well, when the matter came to me I said:	Unless the percentage of consenting bondholders is much higher than seventy-five per cent I do not think it wise to introduce into the Canadian parliament a measure which would have the effect of coercing a considerable number of minority bondholders, and I simply told the company that if they desired to avoid Exchequer court proceedings they would have to get a practically universal assent. I was anxious to avoid the very thing my hon. friend points out, that is, a feeling of soreness, a feeling that people had not been treated properly; and it was not until we were assured of ninety-two per cent of assents that the arrangement now proposed was inserted in the bill. As I said before we would surely have heard of objections to it had there been any, because no matter of a financial character that I can recall has had wider public discussion in the press than this has had. The details we are now discussing have been discussed in the homes of many small investors in the old country, because this issue is very largely held by small investors, as the number of the debenture holders indicates, and it is very well understood, I am quite sure, that we would have heard before this of any substantial ground for complaint, if such had existed.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
I do not wish to labour the point, but it does seem to me very doubtful if many of these small investors know that in this scheme it is proposed that the parliament of Canada should deliberately take away from these people any right they may have; that is to say, we are going to compel them to accept this arrangement whether they want it or not. If these people were united in any way in a company with a majority of ninety-two per cent of them enforcing their will on the rest, that would be a different matter. But it does seem to me that parliament is doing here something that is not right in principle, and something which it is just possible we may be sorry for some day.
Will the minister be kind enough to give us a little information as to just how the Grand Trunk was taken over by the government? As far as I remember that has not been mentioned in the debate.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: The old Grand Trunk?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Yes, as to whether it went into a receivership or what the procedure was.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: My hon. friend is imposing upon me a rather difficult job.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: The minister need only give it very briefly''. I want a point cleared up for my own satisfaction.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
It occurred, of course,
long before I had anything to do with the matter. If I should err in giving an historical review I am subject to correction by gentlemen who were members of the House at the time. The former Grand Trunk was taken over by the government of Canada as the result of arbitration proceedings. Those proceedings decided the amount, if any, that should be paid for the junior stocks, and the road-the former Grand Trunk-is now the absolute property of the government of Canada.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Of the Canadian National Railways.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Of the Canadian National Railways, which in turn are owned by the government of Canada, subject to public charges. What I mean by public charges are such bonds .issued as are outstanding and which embody obligations to the public secured by the property.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: And the rental charges.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
And the rental charges.
What was arbitrated was the value of the preferred and common stock in the old Grand Trunk, the stock being acquired by the Canadian government.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
I should like to know if thi3
clause is in harmony with the provisions of the trust mortgage which secured the bonds in question.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: There was no trust mortgage.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: I think there was.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
If there was not, then it seems to me this provision is more far-reaching. I refer to the words which appear at the top of page 2 of the bill:
All the terms and provisions of the scheme of arrangement shall be binding on all holders of Pacific stock, whether assenting to or not assenting to the scheme of arrangement-
If there was some document which gave certain rights which could be exercised notwithstanding the wishes of the minority, that would be all right; but if there is no such

Grand Trunk Pacific Ry. Co.
right it seems to me there is very grave doubt about it, and it may be an interference with property and civil rights as well. I thought the minister made some reference to a statutory mortgage.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: No, statutory stock.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
Then I misunderstood the
minister. Is it the fact that this arrangement will absolutely deprive these people of rights which they undoubtedly have? I am not seeking to object to the legislation, but the thought comes to me which was first raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). The thought was in my own mind at the time but I imagined it was overcome by virtue of some arrangement with the Pacific bondholders themselves when they purchased the bonds.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: There is.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: If there is such an arrangement that would satisfy me absolutely on the point.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Look at clause 9, subsection (a) of the scheme of arrangement on page 7 of the bill.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Then, as I understand it, that scheme of arrangement is one that was made without the assent of the eight per cent. My point is this: Where do you get the right to interfere at all with the acquired rights of the eight per cent? We know quite well that there are clauses in mortgages securing bonds which give rights where there are certain majorities, but it seems to me that feature is absent here. If it is, what I should like to be enlightened upon .is whether it is proper to deprive these eight per cent, or whatever the percentage is, of their rights, and is it not an interference with property and civil rights?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: The Railway Act and the Exchequer court together provide that in connection with matters of this kind, whenever seventy-five per cent of the bondholders have assented, the Exchequer court may determine to bind the other twenty-five per cent. What parliament is asked to decide on this occasion is whether ninety-two per cent of assents received is sufficient to justify this parliament in saying there is no necessity to go through the extra machinery and to incur the extra expense and delay, which is even more serious, of an Exchequer court action. If I could see that an injury was being done to anyone, I would not suggest such a course; but in view of the very large proportion of assents and the fact also that we are not taking much away from these people, because after all they are getting a guaranteed security-

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: I am not criticising the terms at all; I am referring to the authority.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: It is a gilt-edged security. The other is perpetual and a perpetual source of uncertainty in regard to the receipt of interest. There is no doubt they will receive two per cent interest; the bonds will achieve c definite market value, and a larger proportion of assents has been received, than has ever been known in financial history.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
The question of injury is after all a question to be decided by each person; it is their personal opinion and that is the great danger that confronts us in this case. By right of might, because of course that is the only way in which we can handle the matter in this parliament, this parliament can say that those people's right is taken away and they are given something else in its place. That is wrong in principle and personally I would like to register my objection to it.
I would like to ask the minister another question in regard to the prior claims which the Grand Trunk must pay before they will have to pay these debenture stocks, that is, whether the interest on the money advanced by the government to the Grand Trunk once it was taken over, would be a prior claim.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
I can perhaps best answer that question by reading the exact wording of the conditional guarantee given by the Grand Trunk Railway Company to the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. It reads:
Provided always that the liability of the Grand Trunk in the premises shall from time to time be conditional and wholly depend upon the amount of its gross earnings during any half year ending on some 30th day of June or 31st day of December showing a surplus after the following deductions therefrom (that is to say):
1.	All working expenses as defined by the Canadian acts of parliament relating to the Grand Trunk railway.
2.	All interest and other moneys payable by the Grand Trunk in respect of
(a)	The Grand Trunk loan capital as defined by the said acts.
(b)	Any bonds or liabilities of any other company pursuant to any guarantee or undertaking heretofore given by the Grand Trunk.
That is given prior to this one.
And such surplus as aforesaid being shown the liability of the Grand Trunk in the premises shall be limited to the amount of such surplus and shall wholly determine when a payment or payments to such amount shall have been made to any holder or holders of stock under the covenant in that behalf hereinbefore contained.
It ranks next after the charges created prior to the giving of it.
218	COMMONS
Grand Trunk Pacific Ry. Co.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Am I right in understanding that the bonds outstanding are perpetual debentures and the principal never matures?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Then I am wholly in sympathy with this bill. If eight per cent of the bondholders say: "We do not agree to this proposition ", let them hang on to their bonds and the government continue to pay them the four per cent or whatever interest is payable. The government will never have to pay the principal. Is that not the worst position the Dominion of Canada can be placed in?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: That is why we have that section.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
What was the market
value of the old bonds and what is the market value of the present stock they are getting?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: The new bonds have not yet been issued, but the old ones sold last year at amounts varying from just over sixty to pretty close to seventy at times.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
I should like to congratulate all who have been concerned in completing this arrangement because it is eminently in the interests of this country that it should be done. I say so for two or three reasons. In the first place we are getting quit, within a reasonable time, of these bonds and at the expense of one-half of the interest due those bondholders. In the second place there has been a good deal of dissatisfaction in the old country, whether warranted or not I am not prepared to say, although I have my opinion in regard to the matter. It is eminently in the interests of this country that that source of dissatisfaction be removed and it is being removed by this bill.
We have been very large borrowers in London in years past. In recent years since the war we have been borrowing largely from the United States; but the time may and very likely will arrive and perhaps before long when we shall again have to have recourse to the British financial market. In view of those and other considerations I think it is highly desirable that this question be settled on a fair basis, and the proposal before the House does settle it on an eminently fair basis so far as this country is concerned.
The other point brought up is in regard to the outstanding or possible outstanding eight per cent in value of the bonds concerned. If I am in a company and if ninety-two per cent of my friends have made up their minds that an arrangement proposed to be carried out by the company is fair, right and desirable, I do not think I shall receive very much sympathy, either within the company or on the [Mr. Dunning.!
street, for shouting in regard to my rights having been disregarded. I do not think, as regards arrangements of this kind carried on over a period of years in this country generally, you will find any other such arrangement has been so successfully carried out that ninety^two per cent have acquiesced voluntarily without any coercion of any kind whatsoever. In view of these considerations I am strongly in favour of the passage of this bill.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: If this bill goes through, as it will, and the eight per cent should wish to take action against the government for the payment of what would naturally fall due to them, what stands in their way? I know in some cases permission must be had from the government before action can be taken against it. Is that the situation in this case?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
By law we say here: If
this bill passes, they shall be deemed to have transferred to the company. That is, we are here doing what the Exchequer court would do under our ordinary laws if the matter were placed before it. We are doing it here only because there is such a large proportion of consent in the first place, and because by doing so we can avoid the expense and, what is more important, the delay involved in allowing time for proceedings to be taken before the Exchequer court by any possible dissenter.
I might say something which I have not said before in connection with this bill, namely, that I regard it as the first step towards straightening out the very serious complications of the Canadian national financial structure. I do not know if I shall live to see it completely straightened out, or if I shall be able to handle the job, but there is no question about it that one of the most serious expenses of the Canadian National system, one of the barriers to its success, is its present complicated financial structure, and here we are taking the first essential step in the direction of simplifying that structure. It will enable, as I said before, the Grand Trunk Pacific receivership to be terminated, with all the separate bookkeeping and legal procedure which that has involved. It will enable the Grand Trunk Pacific and its subsidiaries to be merged with the Canadian National system, and until this is done, until this bill is passed and this matter is settled, that amalgamation is impossible. I hope to come later with other proposals to reduce the extent of the confusion that now exists in the Canadian National financing. But it will be a much slower process than some of our editorial friends would have us believe. It is a most complex problem. When I come forward with this one proposal, immediately it bristles with difficul-

Grand Trunk Pacific Ry. Co.
ties, and members of the committee have no trouble at all in pointing out possible difficulties, possible injustices, possible complications. Each one of the financial motions necessary to deal with the situation-and eighty-nine separate corporations now comprise the Canadian National system-will involve, I am afraid discussions of this kind whenever it is necessary to bring them to parliament. This is merely the first step.

speechtext: The minister is not referring to the question of reduction of capitalization, is he?

speechtext:

too far.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: Then why refer to it at all?

speechtext: I understood the minister to say in reply to a question that the worst that could happen with respect to the eight per cent, if they were dissatisfied, would be that they would hold on to their stock.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
No, that would not do
them any good.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: The only advantage then, I take it, in not referring this matter to the Exchequer court and getting an order from them is that it can be done here much more quickly.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES

My hon. friend understands that the Exchequer court would have to give a period of time in their own discretion within which to permit any of these eight per cent to come forward. maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: I wonder if the minister would answer this question. Now that we are facing the possibility of paying interest on this stock, does he not think we are due for a reduction of freight rates in Canada?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext: In the last line but one it says " sinking fund and call ". What is the necessity for the word " call "?

speechtext: Would the minister explain what this clause is for?

speechtext: We provided in section 5 for cremating the securities. Here we are providing for eliminating the charge which the cremated securities carried before they were cremated.

speechtext: The language of this section is similar to the language of section 5. maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
What is the meaning of the words in lines 31, 32 and 33:

speechtext:
The explanation on the
other page of the bill deals with it completely.

speechtext:
We have been referred to the explanation and we would like to look at it.
Winding-up Act

speechtext:
We would like to expedite
business, but. we should be given a chance to read the explanation.

speechtext:
If I understand the
matter correctly, this means that the charge for interest would foe against the Grand Trunk Pacific, notwithstanding the arrangement that is being made with the bondholders on behalf of the Grand Trunk. I think I am safe in saying that the troubles of the Grand Trunk Pacific are due very largely to the management of the Grand Trunk in the location of that railway. It is a fine illustration of bad business management in that regard when we know that the survey was , originally made to the Peace river country, where they neglected about seven hundred miles of good farming territory to build seven hundred miles through bush, ia territory which cannot be revenue-producing. speechtext:
What is the use of carrying
this item on the books? Would it not be just as well to wipe it out?

speechtext: My hon. friend wants to see the Canadian National financing gradually and properly cleared up, but it is necessary in doing it to proceed one step at a time. It will be a book entry merely for 'the time being, and it will maintain the relative standing of the indebtedness between the parties as it now exists. We should not, until we are prepared to look at the whole structure and deal with it, proceed to wipe out individual assets and liabilities and simply forget them.

This question of an adequate audit- has been discussed on several occasions. I appreciate what the minister says, that it is unwise to build up a staff that will simply be a duplication of some other staff, but perhaps this difficulty could be overcome if the Auditor General were appointed the auditor for the board, not necessarily having other auditors duplicating the work. The House ought to bear in mind- and this applies generally-that it is the people who advance these large sums. Montreal is admitted by all to be a well administered port; still, $40,000,000 odd is spent there. In my own city of Vancouver I presume, speaking offhand, about $15,000,000 is spent. Now that is money advanced by the people of Canada. These two harbour commissions pay the interest on these advances and provide for sinking fund. That is very good; it is highly commendable. On the other hand is it not reasonable that those who advance the money should have an opportunity in some manner of determining whether or not it is properly expended? When harbour commissioners appoint their own auditors, it is just the same as the management of a company appointing the auditors and the shareholders having nothing to do with their appointment. I pointed out last year-it as a principle not always followed, but it is a sound and a vital principle-that in the administration of all corporate bodies the shareholders appoint, or are supposed to appoint, the auditor, and the auditor is supposed to be the safeguarder of the shareholders' interest as between them and the management. So I suggest, as I have suggested before-and I say now in support of the suggestion of the hon. member for West Calgary-that the shareholders, represented by this parliament, should really be the appointees of the auditor, namely, the Auditor General of Canada. The great respect in which the institution of Auditor General is generally held throughout Canada is based upon the fulness of the report which he from year to year presents to parliament, and upon the freedom which parliament is allowed to scrutinize that report. We contend, and I am wholly in accord with the suggestion, that it would be better if the Auditor General were constituted the auditor of the harbour boards.

I should like to endorse the position that has just been taken by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre
with regard to the question of auditing. I recall several years ago, when some of us were urging bank inspection, that the then Minister of Finance took the position that the ground was covered when the government were able under the existing arrangements to send in an inspector whenever they deemed it advisable. That is precisely the ground that has been taken this afternoon by the Minister of Finance with regard to the audit question. Many hon. members will recall that after that position had been taken regarding bank inspection there occurred the failure of the Home Bank, which brought home to the public at large the necessity for a more adequate system of inspection. It was then provided that the government should assume responsibility for inspection. It had been stated that if there were a government inspector, a very large staff would have to be employed. I think it was later recognized that this was not essential, and legislation was passed providing for the appointment of am inspector-general who would have charge in a general way of all inspection. It seems a very reasonable thing that something of this kind should be done with regard to these important commissions. I do not know why there should even need to be a duplication of auditors. If the auditing is to be done by the government it would be quite unnecessary that the harbour board should have its own auditors. I gladly support the position already taken.

It seems to me the proposal advanced that the Auditor General should do the work of the harbour commission is so logical and reasonable that it should not be necessary to say anything more in favour of it, except to commend it to the good judgment of the members of the government. Rather than involve extra expense it would probably save a good deal of money, because if the Auditor General were the official auditor for the harbour commission the Finance minister would certainly never 'be called upon to send out auditors under the audit board. So that there would be distinct saving, and as I know the Finance minister is always looking for a place to save something in the way of expenditure, I gladly commend the scheme to him and hope it will receive the approval of the government.

I shall preface that request with some very brief observations. During the last week the House has witnessed a spirit of courtesy and co-operation which I think has been unparalleled in my seventeen sessions in parliament. We have expedited, or tried to expedite, the passage of the various measures. This afternoon we advanced several important bills for the Minister of Finance with scarcely any comment, and I must say that the ministry have been very prompt in making brief statements and explanations of the various measures introduced. This fact we welcome and appreciate. Now, speaking for myself alone I am exceedingly anxious that we should expedite the business of this session. We hlave had a couple of years of pretty hard parliamentary duty, and I think both the country and parliament will be the better for a little surcease from bitterness and controversy. I can say on behalf of my colleagues on this side that we have tendered our hearty co-operation and, as far as we could extend it, courtesy in these matters, and I should be very sorry to see this spirit dissipated in any way. It takes two to make a bargain as well as two to make a quarrel, and if we have a response from the ministry such as we have had during tire past few days I think we can assure them of reasonable co-operation. Of course we reserve always our right to question and criticise measures-and I may 'add that the ministry will find a keen and critical opposition very often a very valuable factor.
I would remind the committee that last year this particular measure was perhaps one of the-I was going to say the most poorly drafted measures introduced. I am not placing the blame upon the minister who had the bill in charge, because there are officers of the House who are supposed to assist in the drafting of these measures; but last year I recall that the whole House was engaged, sitting after sitting, in correcting the drafting of the bill that was presented to it. It was very faulty drafting, and the minister withdrew it two or three times and had certain sections redrafted. That is what occasioned the query regarding the drafting of the present resolution, and while the point has been referred to already I should like to allude to it again. It is quite clear to me that the wording of the resolution, and of this particular clause as it now reads-it has not yet been formally changed-namely, "the diminution in the present value" is a meaningless term, or a term that certainly does not fit in with the intent of the proposed legislation. The intent is to provide for the
diminution of the difference between the original price and what the price may be at a given time fixed by parliament, which is an altogether different thing. Had it specified a diminution in the purchase price, which would be the exact reverse of the present reading there might be some sense in it, but as the provision now reads it has no sense. What I want to ask the minister is this: In the light of his assertion that this is the same measure that was introduced last session-and I think he described it as the same resolution and the same bill which had passed both houses of parliament-how does he explain the resolution of last year as compared with this one? There is very little resemblance between them. This resolution consists of .three very short clauses; the resolution last year occupied a whole page and contained seven different specified clauses. Furthermore, certain matters which were referred to in the resolution last year are not referred to in the present resolution. Now, Mr. Chairman, had we accepted the minister's statement and passed this resolution we would have been more or less precluded from offering criticism later with respect to the difference between the two resolutions. The minister should explain to the committee what changes there are in this resolution from the preceding one and the reasons for the changes.
I have no doubt they are sound and probably an improvement, because the original resolution of last year, with the bill based thereon, was certainly far from a perfect measure. retraction. Now let us go back and see when these lands were bought. They were bought in the years 1919 and 1920, and some of them a little later. It was said by some that they were valued by officials of the government. They were not valued by officials of the government, but iby a representative board that was appointed. No doubt the members of that board were recommended to the govertrmeint of the day by friends of the latter. They put a valuation upon these lands and they valued them too high. This govern-

Soldier Settlement Act
ment was not responsible. This government, ever since 1922, has endeavoured to respond to the reasonable requests of the committee that looked carefully into the matter. This is the third attempt we have made to bring in legislation to correct the high (prices paid for land at that time. If the legislation has been delayed it has not been delayed by the government of the day. The legislation may be improved, it may not be ideal, but it is an honest attempt on the part of the government to meet the wishes of the joint committee that made certain recommendations.
It is all wrong to have the impression go out ito the country that the land was bought by the government of the day at exorbitant prices. That as not the case. A great deal of the land was purchased at fair prices, at reasonable prices; indeed some of it was sold for more than the soldier settler paid for it. But there are a few districts-and I think I know something of the matter because I was in that department-throughout Canada where the land was bought at high prices. The price of the land was beyond its value, as it was not suitable for agriculture; it was unloaded on the poor settler to the advantage of some friends who were able, 'at the time, to get the ear of the government. I am not blaming the government. In a large country like this the government in Ottawa cannot be watching everything. Generally speaking; I repeat, the land was bought at a fair price, and I may say that as Minister of Finance I will watch pretty closely to see whether any attempt is made to reimburse some chaps who have made fairly good on the- land. It seems to me that we would do well ito let the resolution go through as it is. When the bill is presented, and we sit down in committee to consider it, if the measure should contain any errors we can correct them.

Senate; it passed the Senate in an amended form; it came back to this House and it would have passed here. never be able to pass a bill that will meet all the cases and1 hardships that have occurred.

The minister rather insinuated that the purpose of my remarks was delay. There is one rather peculiar thing about the minister that has struck me, and that is his peculiar veneration for the Senate since the beginning of the present session.

There have been remarks, Mr. Chairman, about the past history of this measure, and I thought it worth while to get the facts. We are all relying on our memories in connection with a rather hectic period last, summer. I find that the then acting Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment in the person of the present member for Fort William,, introduced this measure on its being returned amended from the Senate, and Hansard of last session very clearly sets out what was the attitude of 'hon. gentlemen opposite, who then composed what has since been described as the "shadow government", towards this principle of permitting the Exchequer court to be the deciding factor, and also towards the general principles of this legislation. It is interesting to note that the concluding exercises in connection with this particular measure last session consisted of a further effort on the part of the Acting Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment to get the House to pass the bill as it came from the Senate, and he was met with the objection by my right hon. leader that we on our side of the House had not yet had time to consider fully the changes proposed by the Senate, and we asked for time, at least until after the six o'clock recess, to look into the proposed changes. It is interesting to note that this matter never came up again. Other very important matters came up. Now, Mr. Chairman, we on this side of the House have had time to consider the effect of the changes proposed last year by my hon. friends opposite, and we now come here and say we agree. Coming here in a spirit of agreement, we now find our hon. friends opposite have changed their minds again, and they want something different.
So far as the Exchequer court is concerned, if it were to be used as a court in the city of Ottawa to adjudicate on the value of soldier settler lands, of course that would be an

Why not give us the

I understand that the purpose of the resolution is to give an opportunity to discuss the principles which will be at a later date embodied in the bill to be presented to parliament, and therefore I presume that what I have to say will be in order, 'as it deals (with the principle of the bill.
I assume that it is the intention of the government in bringing in this legislation to give immediate and effective relief to the soldier settlers. The soldier settlers at the present time are rather afraid that the process of arriving at a revaluation is going to be so cumbersome and so difficult to attain, and perhaps so expensive, as to nullify the beneficial effects of the legislation, and accordingly many soldier settlers are of the opinion that it would be better not to attempt revaluation as it is suggested in this resolution and as was provided for in the bill of last year, but rather to make to all soldier settlers now on the land, a flat percentage reduction in the purchase price. It is not my intention to argue that now, I merely pass the suggestion on to the minister in the hope that he will give it consideration before he finally drafts the bill. I think it is clear that no legislation can possibly meet every case. It will be absolutely impossible under any proposal to give relief to everybody, but if we

Soldier Settlement Act
have a 'bill which provides for a very difficult process of revaluation, it may be that many who could get relief under the simple proposal of the soldiers to have a flat percentage reduction wild not get any relief at all. I offer this suggestion to the minister, and I hope that he will give it his serious consideration when he prepares the legislation which is to be based on the resolution before the committee.

I take it for granted-and
if I am taking too much for granted I hope the Minister of Immigration and Colonization will say so-that the bill will be brought down and introduced in the same spirit as it was presented a year ago; that is, thait the minister is willing to consider any changes which members of the House may suggest when they have the bill before them. At the present time I am very much concerned with reference to the proposal to accept the amendment which the Senate proposed last year, of having the valuation in some cases referred to the Exchequer court. Many soldier settlers feel that their cases are practically hopeless if they have to go to such a body as the Exchequer court of Canada, situated, as they are, two thousand miles from Ottawa. The hon. member from Dauphin made a splendid suggestion-and I hope the minister will accept it-thiat when the bill comes down it be sent to a special committee, or one of the select committees of the House which is capable of dealing with the bill in a satisfactory manner.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It would
be regrettable if in the matter of legislation regarding soldiers the government should take the position that they would not consider any suggested changes. That was not our attitude last year, nor the attitude of any party in this House; but rather that the House should endeavour to reconcile the differences as nearly as they could with respect to this particular measure and enact legislation that would be mutually beneficial, or beneficial to the soldiers themselves. I want to assure hon. members opposite that the same consideration will be given to suggestions as has been given heretofore. I can quite understand the difficulty that my hon. friend experiences. This revaluation is long overdue, and many men have been forced to leave their land who, if the revaluation had taken place two years ago, would now be farming on it. We want at this session of parliament to pass a bill that will provide for a revaluation of the land and play fair with the men still on the land. I think we can surely approach this question in that spirit. I can foresee that a lot of argument made last year is going to be introduced again this year, but there is no harm in that. That is what this body is for. I hope the outcome will be that the suggestions made will be beneficial to the soldiers and that we will enact a measure that will be of real value to the men who are fighting their way along on land that was valued too high, or sold to them at a high price. Do not forget that many of these men were fortunate in their selections and that their land is now worth more than when they purchased it. I say that to show how impossible the suggestion made by the hon. member for Wetaski-win would be. We havg gone over all that, and when hon. members know the circumstances surrounding these cases they will realize that some of these suggestions would not be beneficial. As one member of the government I hope the discussion will continue in the way it has hitherto been conducted in connection with soldier settlement matters and that we will arrive at a proper conclusion.

Long Term Farm Loans
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Forke thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 61, to amend the Soldier Settlement Act, 1919.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved,-1. That there shall be a board known as the Canadian Farm Loan Board which shall be a body politic and corporate consisting of four members, one of whom shall be the Minister of Finance and the other three shall be appointed by the governor in council and of the latter one shall be designated by the Canadian Farm Loan commissioners.
2.	That the board shall issue farm loan bonds to make long term loans to farmers, and the government of Canada shall provide initial capital for the board to an amount not exceeding five million dollars and subscribe an amount of 5 per cent of the capital stock as loans are made by the board.
3.	That the government of each province in which loans are made shall be required to subscribe to the capital stock of the board as loans are made in such province an amount equal to 5 per cent of the said loans and each borrower an amount of 5 per cent of his loan payable at the time the loan is made. The loans shall be made on the security of first mortgage on farm lands; the interest rate shall be such a rate in excess of the interest payable on the farm loan bonds as is sufficient to provide for the expenses of operation; the farm loan bonds shall be legal investments and may be purchased by the Minister of Finance provided that the amount of such bonds held by him shall not at any time exceed $15,000,000; and the amount of any payment by the government of Canada on account of capital of the board or as payment for farm loan bonds purchased shall be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund on the authority of the governor in council.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
